Source: Congressional Research Service. 
Note: Under each act, the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) had to set up a process for clergy members to file the revocation, which typically took several months. For example, to implement the Ticket to Work and Work Incentives Improvement Act of 1999, the IRS released the relevant form (Form 2031) in April 2000. 
Social Security Benefits for Clergy Members
Workers become eligible for Social Security benefits for themselves and their family members through employment covered by Social Security. To qualify for Social Security retired-worker benefits, a worker generally must earn 40 credits, equivalent to 10 years of covered employment. Fewer credits are required to qualify for Social Security disability benefits, with the number varying according to the worker’s age at the onset of disability. A worker’s initial monthly benefit amount is based on average earnings over his or her career in covered employment. For example, retired-worker benefits are calculated using the worker’s 35 years of highest indexed covered earnings.
Clergy members who elect Social Security coverage generally need 10 years of covered employment to qualify for retired-worker benefits. Earnings from nonministerial work covered by Social Security also count toward this requirement. In general, workers with more years of covered earnings may receive higher initial monthly benefits because additional earnings are included in the benefit calculation.
Clergy members with no or limited Social Security-covered earnings may qualify for auxiliary benefits based on another individual’s earnings record. These benefits may be payable to eligible spouses, former spouses, survivors, children, or parents of a worker covered by Social Security.
Social Security Windfall Elimination Provision (WEP)
From 1984 through 2023, clergy members’ Social Security benefits could have been reduced by the WEP if they had earnings from both Social Security-covered and noncovered employment and received pension benefits based on their noncovered earnings. The Social Security Fairness Act of 2023 (P.L. 118-273) repealed the WEP and the Government Pension Offset for monthly benefits payable after December 2023. Accordingly, beginning in 2024, the WEP no longer applies to Social Security benefits, including those received by clergy members who elected Social Security coverage.

The Clergy Act (H.R. 227)
The Clergy Act (P.L. 119-125), signed into law on October 20, 2026, provides clergy members with another limited opportunity to revoke a previously elected exemption from SECA taxes. Eligible clergy members may revoke their exemptions by filing a revocation during the period beginning after enactment (subject to the IRS’s implementation process) and ending on the due date of their federal income tax return for their second taxable year beginning after December 31, 2028 (expected to generally be April 15, 2031, but could be different with extensions or changes). The revocation may take effect in either the 2029 or 2030 tax year as specified in the application. Once effective, the revocation is irrevocable. The act also directs the IRS to develop a plan to notify eligible clergy members of this opportunity, helping ensure they are aware of their ability to participate in Social Security and potentially qualify for related retirement benefits.
Clergy members who revoke their exemptions will pay SECA taxes on their ministerial earnings for the remainder of their working years and may subsequently qualify for Social Security and Medicare benefits. Additional years of covered earnings may also increase their Social Security benefits. As a result, the law is expected to increase revenues (and thus reduce federal deficits) in the near term and increase outlays (and thus increase federal deficits) in later decades.
The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) estimates that approximately 3,000 clergy members would reverse their decisions in 2029 or 2030, resulting in an $84 million increase in payroll tax revenues over the 2026-2036 period. Of that amount, an estimated $68 million would come from additional Social Security payroll taxes and $16 million from additional Medicare payroll taxes. 
CBO estimates that outlays for Social Security and Medicare benefits would each increase by $1 million over the 2026-2036 period as a result of those reversals. Most of the additional benefits attributable to the reversals would be paid after 2036.
CBO also estimates that implementing the legislation, including reporting to Congress on efforts to inform clergy members about their eligibility to elect coverage, would increase the IRS’s administrative costs by less than $500,000. Such spending would be subject to the availability of appropriated funds.

api_metadata.summary:
On July 4, 2026, the United States celebrated the semiquincentennial (250th) anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence. As part of the celebration, Congress authorized two time capsules—one for Philadelphia, PA, to be placed near Independence Hall, and one for Washington, DC, to be placed in the U.S. Capitol. In addition to these authorizations, this In Focus also discusses past official time capsules to celebrate milestone anniversaries of the Declaration of Independence.
Over the ages, time capsules have captured the popular mind ... Time capsules are about sending out slices of our time to the future. 
All successful time capsules must evoke ... a real sense of immediacy with a given period of historical-cultural space-time, supplied by a wide variety of significant human details, mundane, grandiose or both.
—William E. Jarvis, Time Capsules: A Cultural History 
(McFarland & Co., 2003), pp. 2, 16.
Semiquincentennial Time Capsules
To celebrate the semiquincentennial anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence, Congress authorized two capsules—one in Philadelphia, PA and one in Washington, DC.
Philadelphia Time Capsule
In 2016, Congress authorized the U.S. Semiquincentennial Commission (America250) to create a time capsule containing “a representative portion of all books, manuscripts, miscellaneous printed matter, memorabilia, relics, and other materials relating to the United States Semiquincentennial,” to be buried on Independence Mall on July 4, 2026, and unearthed on the 500th anniversary of the United States on July 4, 2276 (P.L. 114-196, §7(f)). 
“America’s Time Capsule” was built by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) and was buried on July 4, 2026, at Independence National Historical Park in Philadelphia. The semiquincentennial time capsule contains submissions from each state, the District of Columbia, and each territory. Other submissions originate from America250 and its partner organizations, including the International Olympic Committee and NBC’s TODAY Show, the Library of Congress, Major League Baseball, the National Basketball Association, the National Endowment for the Arts, the National Football League, the National Hockey League, NIST, the Professional Golfers’ Association (PGA) of America and the PGA Tour, the Smithsonian Institution, and the Supreme Court of the United States. Figure 1 shows “America’s Time Capsule” at the burial ceremony in Philadelphia, PA.
Figure 1. America’s Time Capsule, Philadelphia
/
Source: America250, “America250 Time Capsule,” July 5, 2026.
Congressional Time Capsule
In 2026, Congress authorized the creation of a time capsule and its burial in the U.S. Capitol Visitor Center (P.L. 119-79). The time capsule was unveiled on June 24, 2026, and put on display in Emancipation Hall (H.Con.Res. 109). At the ceremony, Speaker of the House Mike Johnson noted that “In many ways, the Congressional Time Capsule is a reflection of our faith in the future of this grand experiment in self-governance, faith that this moment is worth preserving, and faith that the great American story will endure for another 250 years.”
The Congressional Time Capsule’s legislation (P.L. 119-79) specified that the capsule is to include “a single, joint letter” from congressional leadership and any other item that leadership jointly determines appropriate. The Architect of the Capitol issued a series of Dear Colleague letters about contents of the time capsule. For a list of contributions from congressional delegations, see https://www.visitthecapitol.gov/tc-kiosk-embed. Specific burial plans for the Congressional Time Capsule have yet to be announced. The time capsule is scheduled to be opened on July 4, 2276, during the 244th Congress (P.L. 119-79, §2(d)). Figure 2 shows the Congressional Time Capsule on display in Emancipation Hall of the Capitol Visitor Center. 
Figure 2. Congressional Time Capsule, U.S. Capitol Visitor Center
/
Source: U.S. Capitol (@visitthecapitol), X post, July 23, 2026.
Past Anniversary Time Capsules
At least two previous milestone anniversaries of the Declaration of Independence involved time capsules as part of the celebration—for the 1876 centennial and the 1976 bicentennial.
Centennial (1876)
In 1876, Philadelphia hosted the Centennial Exhibition to celebrate the 100th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence. For the 1876 Centennial Exposition, Mrs. Anna Deihm, widow of Civil War veteran Charles F. Deihm, facilitated the creation of a safe to be filled with memorabilia from the centennial celebrations. In 1879, Deihm offered the safe as a gift to the United States, with the expectation that it would be opened in 1976 by the President of the United States. In February 1879, Congress held a ceremony in the Capitol to formally close the safe. On January 19, 1976, at the beginning of the 2nd session of the 94th Congress (1975-1976), Representatives and Senators attended a ceremony to open the outer doors of the safe, which was then put on display for public viewing. Figure 3 shows the Centennial Safe as opened by President Ford in 1976.
Figure 3. Centennial Safe
/
Source: Warren K. Leffler, Mrs. Charles F. Deihm’s “Centennial Safe” Kept at the U.S. Capitol and Opened by President Gerald Ford as Part of the United States Bicentennial, photograph, Library of Congress, June 23, 1976.
Bicentennial (1976)
For the bicentennial anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence, the congressionally authorized American Revolution Bicentennial Administration (P.L. 93-179) created the National Bicentennial Time Capsule “as a bicentennial gift to the United States.” The National Bicentennial Time Capsule was 1 of 56 time capsules made by the Reynolds Metals Company, which, according to media reports, gave one to each state and territory. The National Bicentennial Time Capsule is stored by the National Archives and Records Administration and is scheduled to be opened on July 4, 2075. Figure 4 shows the National Bicentennial Time Capsule.
Figure 4. National Bicentennial Time Capsule
/
Source: American Revolution Bicentennial Administration, “National Bicentennial Time Capsule,” National Archives and Records Administration, 1976.
For more information on congressional celebrations of milestone anniversaries of the Declaration of Independence, see CRS Report R48473, Congressional Involvement in the Celebration of Anniversaries of the Declaration of Independence, by Jacob R. Straus.
